title: The graded quiz, replayed
intro: The course's end-of-course quiz — 10 questions with the official explanations. Score to beat: your original 100/100.

questions.prompt: The main advantage of SDD vs vibe coding is…
choices: SDD uses persistent specs to anchor intent across sessions, avoiding the drift of long prompt dialogues
SDD requires writing all code manually, using the agent only for small suggestions
SDD lets the agent work fully autonomously with no human review
SDD eliminates the need for version control since specs replace git history
questions.explanation: Persistent specs anchor the agent's work so you can make large changes confidently — no mental load of tracking a messy chat history.

choices: README.md, CHANGELOG.md, LICENSE.md
user-stories.md, acceptance-criteria.md, sprint-backlog.md
mission.md, tech-stack.md, and roadmap.md
requirements.md, plan.md, validation.md
questions.explanation: The three pillars: the why (mission.md), the how (tech-stack.md), and the when (roadmap.md). The fourth option is the FEATURE-spec triple — the classic trap.

choices: README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, CHANGELOG.md
design.md, code.md, tests.md
plan.md, requirements.md, and validation.md
mission.md, tech-stack.md, roadmap.md
questions.explanation: plan.md lays out the task groups, requirements.md captures scope & decisions, validation.md defines how you'll know the feature is done. Constitution = project level; feature spec = per feature.

questions.prompt: The three phases of the feature cycle are…
choices: Design, Code, Ship
Plan, Implement, Validate
Specify, Compile, Test
Research, Write, Deploy
questions.explanation: Three repeatable phases per feature — and between features you also replan to refine the constitution.

questions.prompt: The developer's role in SDD is best described as…
choices: An architect and reviewer who provides the spec and steers the agent, which handles most implementation
A project manager who only creates tickets and never touches code or specs
A QA tester whose only job is finding bugs in the agent's output
A typist who writes most production code by hand
questions.explanation: The agent is the muscle, the spec is the brain. You define intent, review results, and steer.

questions.prompt: Why route changes through the agent instead of editing files yourself?
choices: To save context tokens in the agent's memory
To prevent drift — the agent updates the related specs at the same time, keeping docs and code in sync
Because manually editing code is always slower
Because developers aren't allowed to touch code in an SDD project
questions.explanation: Editing code directly risks leaving specs and READMEs out of sync; routing changes through the agent keeps everything aligned.

choices: Replanning is optional and most teams skip it to ship faster
It's a chance to reflect, update the constitution and roadmap, and refine your workflow — a normal step, not a failure
Replanning means throwing out the constitution and rewriting from scratch
Replanning is only needed when something has gone badly wrong
questions.explanation: Run slow to run fast: a pause to refine the constitution, tune your process, and set the next feature up for success.

questions.prompt: Can SDD be applied to a legacy codebase?
choices: No — SDD is only for greenfield projects; legacy code needs a rewrite
Both: on a legacy project the agent reverse-engineers a constitution from the existing code and docs, then the normal workflow continues
Only for small personal projects
Only for projects originally started with an AI agent
questions.explanation: Brownfield SDD: the agent explores the codebase, drafts an honest constitution (including gaps), and you proceed with the identical feature loop.

questions.prompt: A 'skill' is… (and when should you create one?)
choices: A reusable package of instructions and resources giving the agent a repeatable capability — create one when you catch yourself retyping the same prompt
A special kind of AI model only certain commercial agents support
A paid plugin bought from an app store
A type of spec that replaces plan/requirements/validation
questions.explanation: Writing the same long prompt repeatedly (like the feature-spec interview)? Turn it into a skill the agent can invoke on demand.

questions.prompt: Why is an agent-agnostic workflow valuable?
choices: Agent-agnostic workflows run measurably faster
The agent landscape moves fast — keeping specs and tools independent of any single agent lets you switch without rebuilding your workflow
It means you never need a coding agent at all
It's required by law for enterprise software
questions.explanation: Standards like Skills, MCP, and ACP keep the SDD process intact when a better agent arrives — your specs move with you.

choices: The interest you pay on cloud compute
The mental load of tracking what the code does and how it evolved — which specs exist to remove
The number of tokens the agent has consumed
Technical debt that only affects senior engineers
questions.explanation: Keep changes manageable and specs in sync to stay fast, in control, and low-debt — cognitive debt is what returns when drift sets in.
